cards.text: Psalm 149 kicks off with "Hallelujah!" The psalmist calls God's people to sing to the LORD a new song. A NEW song, friend, not the same three songs you've had on repeat in the car since forever.

cards.question: The psalmist calls God's people to sing the LORD a new song. Where does he want God's praise sung?

answers.text: In the assembly of the godly
In the council of the elders

cards.text: Next, Israel is called to rejoice in their Maker, and in the same breath the psalmist calls Him their King. Me? My maker's a mystery, friend. I came out of a clearance bin with a 25 cent sticker on my FACE.

cards.question: The psalmist calls God Israel's Maker and their King. Who does he call to rejoice in their King?

cards.text: Then the psalmist gets specific about HOW God's people should praise. No guesswork, friend. It's like a boss who actually explains the assignment. RARE. Beautiful. Somebody frame it.

cards.question: How does the psalmist want God's people to praise His name?

cards.text: Dancing, tambourine AND harp. I can't play either one, friend, and my only dance move is hopping on this gold base. HOP. That's the whole routine.
Why all the dancing and tambourines? The psalmist stops and gives the reason. And friend, this reason? THIS reason? Hold onto your apron.

cards.question: True or false: the psalmist says the LORD takes pleasure in His people.

cards.text: And the LORD adorns the afflicted, the ones worn down and hurting. Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer with blurry edges, so I wasn't just afflicted, I was the CAPTAIN of afflicted.

cards.question: The LORD dresses up the afflicted. He adorns them with ___.

cards.text: Then the psalmist calls for people to exult in glory, and he even picks the spot for the shouting: upon their beds. Not the stage. Not the stadium. The BED.

cards.question: Who does the psalmist call to exult in glory and shout for joy upon their beds?

cards.text: Most of us lie in bed going over the bills. The psalmist calls the saints to lie there shouting for JOY, and then the psalm turns serious.

cards.question: The psalmist says may God's high praises be in the saints' mouths, and may a ___ be in their hands.
True or false: the psalmist pictures the saints' sword being used to inflict vengeance on the nations.
The psalmist pictures the nations' nobles in shackles of iron. Who else does he picture bound with chains?

cards.text: All of this is to execute the judgment written against them. Then the psalmist uses a word I did NOT see coming, friend: he calls it an honor.

cards.question: The psalmist calls carrying out the judgment written against the nations an honor. Who does he say this honor is for?

findings.problem: Story cards 3, 5, 7, 8 and 12 each exceed two sentences. Card 5, for example, runs to six short sentences, and card 12 has four.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Saying that the 25-cent sticker was on Papa Dorin's face adds a new detail to his backstory. The provided story says that he was in a bin at the closing bakery and had a 25-cent price sticker, but does not place that sticker on his face.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The card explicitly uses the dancing and tambourines from verse 3 as well as the reason introduced in verse 4, but it cites only Psalm 149:4. Its citation needs to begin with the first verse it uses.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Too many choices depend on guessing an unrevealed detail. Cards 2, 4 and 6 are detail-discovery questions, while cards 11, 15 and 16 also lack enough context for a reasoned answer. Consequently, most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses, and the discoveries amount to more than a few.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: The setup says only that the LORD adorns or dresses up the afflicted. Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason out "salvation"; the baker must guess the unseen wording from three possibilities.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Saying only that the psalm "turns serious" gives no reasoned path from praises in the saints' mouths to a sword in their hands. Choosing sword rather than scroll or torch is therefore a guess at an unseen detail.
